faq: Which tools can an agent connect to?
Gmail, Outlook, Google Drive, Notion, Slack, common CRMs, Shopify, calendars and any tool with a usable connection. We confirm each one before you order if yours is unusual.
Will you ask for my passwords?
No. You add us as a collaborator, create an agent account, or approve a connection inside the tool. Keys are stored in a secure vault and you can revoke them at any time.
Can the agent delete or send things?
Only if you allow it. We start with read-only access and add send or edit rights one by one. Risky actions can also be paired with the Human Approval service.
What does it cost to run these connections?
Our price covers the set-up. Any subscriptions, API fees or vault costs are billed to you by the providers, and we list them for you before we begin.

desc:
Safe tool access for AI agents connects your agent to email, files, calendar and CRM with the narrowest permissions that still let it work. Ecom Swift LLC sets up each connection, tests it, documents it and shows you how to switch it off.

## Why wide access is the biggest agent risk

An agent is only useful when it can reach your tools. It is only safe when it reaches little more than it needs. Many setups skip the second part: the agent is connected with a personal login or an admin key because that was the fastest way to get it working.

That shortcut means a confused agent, or a malicious instruction hidden in an email, can reach everything the owner can. The damage is not limited to one task. Narrow access limits the harm of any mistake to the small area the agent was meant to use.

## What does safe tool access mean?

Safe tool access means each connection follows the principle of least privilege: the agent gets only the rights it needs, on only the data it needs, and nothing else. A task that needs to read invoices gets read-only access to the invoice folder, not full control of the whole drive.

It also means the access is visible and reversible. You can see what each connection allows, from your own accounts, and you can turn it off at any time without breaking anything else.

## How access design affects safety and usefulness

Good access design makes an agent both safer and easier to trust. When the permissions are small and clear, a manager can approve the agent with confidence, and a wrong action is limited in reach. Narrow access also makes problems easier to trace, because each connection has one purpose.

Usefulness need not suffer. Most tasks need far less access than people assume. Giving the agent a separate account in each tool also helps, since its actions show up under its own name and are not mixed with a person's work.

## What a good tool setup includes

- A list of the tools the agent needs and the reason for each.
- Read-only access wherever the task does not require writing.
- Access limited to named folders, lists, calendars or labels.
- A separate agent account in each tool, not a personal login.
- Keys and tokens kept in a secure store rather than in a prompt or a shared document.
- A test of what the agent should be able to do, and of what it should fail to reach.
- Logging of tool calls, so you can see what was touched and when.
- A one-page access map showing every connection at a glance.
- Written steps for switching each connection off.
- A plan for rotating keys when someone leaves or a key is exposed.

## What we do

We start with a short review of what the agent must do, and list the least access that supports it. For each tool, we create the connection in your own account, using a dedicated agent user where the platform allows it, and limit it to the folders, records or actions that matter.

We then test twice. First we check that the agent can do its job. Then we check that it cannot do what it should not, such as opening a private folder or deleting a record. We document the result in an access map and guide. The Basic package connects a small number of tools. Standard adds more tools, separate agent accounts and the access map. Premium adds a secure key store, full call logging and a safety review of each connection.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Give the agent its own account in each tool.
- Start with read-only access and add write rights only where needed.
- Limit access to the specific folders or lists the task uses.
- Keep keys out of prompts, chat messages and shared documents.
- Review who and what has access on a regular schedule.

**Avoid:**
- Connecting the agent through an owner or administrator login.
- Sharing a password so the agent can "just log in".
- Granting delete rights when the task only reads.
- Leaving old connections active after a project ends.
- Reusing one key across several agents and tools.

## Who this is for

This service suits a business that wants an agent to read and sort an inbox without exposing the whole mailbox. It suits a team connecting an agent to a CRM and a shared drive who want a clear record of what it can touch. It also suits an owner who built a working prototype with broad access and now wants it tightened before real use.

## What we need from you

Tell us which tools the agent should use and what it should do in each. Give us collaborator, team member or developer access in those tools, wherever the platform supports it, so we can create the agent's own connection. We never ask for your passwords, and every connection can be seen and switched off from your own accounts.
